title: Psalm 142: A Prayer from the Cave
summary: Hiding in a cave, David cries aloud to the LORD and pours out his complaint. His spirit is faint, a trap lies along his path, and no one cares for his life. He declares that the LORD is his refuge and his portion in the land of the living, and asks to be set free from his prison so that he can praise God's name among the righteous.
story: Psalm 142 is the third of four prayers for rescue (Psalms 140 to 143) in the Psalter's last collection of David's psalms. It is the only one of the four whose heading ties it to a scene from David's life. After the wider prayers of Psalms 140 and 141, which describe traps and enemies in general terms, Psalm 142 places the reader inside a cave with a man who has lost every human support. Its closing hope that the righteous will gather around him anticipates the confident praise that the collection reaches in Psalms 144 and 145. It is followed by Psalm 143, the last of the seven psalms that Christian tradition has called penitential.
historical:
The heading reads “A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave. A prayer.” Two episodes in 1 Samuel fit. After fleeing from Saul and then from Achish king of Gath, David hid in the cave of Adullam, where his family and a band of about four hundred distressed, indebted, and discontented men gathered to him (1 Samuel 22:1-2). Later, in the wilderness of En-gedi, David and his men hid deep inside a cave that Saul himself entered, and David spared Saul's life (1 Samuel 24). Psalm 57 has a similar heading, “when he fled from Saul into the cave.” The heading of Psalm 142 does not say which cave is meant.

Scholars debate the historical headings of the Psalms. Many conservative scholars take them as reliable ancient tradition. Many others consider them later notes, added by editors who connected the psalms with suitable moments in David's story to help readers pray them. Either way, the heading invites the reader to hear this psalm in the voice of a hunted man with nowhere to go, and the psalm fits that setting closely. Its closing hope that the righteous will gather around him reads naturally against the men who gathered to David at Adullam.
cultural:
The hill country of Judah, especially the limestone wilderness near the Dead Sea, is full of caves. They were used for shelter, storage, burial, and hiding. En-gedi, an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, lies among cliffs honeycombed with caves. For a fugitive, a cave was both a refuge and a trap: safe while no one knew he was there, deadly if he was found.

The right hand (verse 4) was where an advocate or protector would stand, especially in a law court or battle. When the psalmist looks to his right and sees no one, he is saying he has no defender. His confession that the LORD is his portion (verse 5) draws on Israel's land allotment. Each tribe and family received a portion of land as its inheritance, but the priests and Levites received none; the LORD said he himself would be their portion (Numbers 18:20). The psalmist claims the same: with no land, no allies, and no safety, God himself is his share.
literary: Psalm 142 is a short individual lament of seven verses. It begins with two parallel lines describing the act of crying out (verses 1 and 2), then describes the distress: a faint spirit, a hidden trap, no one at his right hand, no refuge, no one who cares (verses 3 and 4). The turn comes in verse 5, where the psalmist answers his own statement that there is no refuge with the confession that the LORD is his refuge. Verses 6 and 7 close with pleas and a vow to praise. The word refuge ties the psalm's hinge together: in verse 4 there is none, and in verse 5 there is one, the LORD himself. The word Maskil in the heading is of uncertain meaning; it may mean a contemplative or instructive psalm, or a skillful song.

outline.t: Crying out and pouring out the complaint
No one at my right hand, no refuge
You are my refuge and my portion
Rescue me from prison so I may praise

doctrines.note: Pouring out a complaint to God is not a failure of faith; it is a form of it. The psalmist brings his fear and loneliness directly to the LORD, trusting him with the whole truth.

The psalm names isolation as one of suffering's sharpest forms: no one sees, no one cares, no one stands beside. It answers not with an explanation but with the presence of God, who knows the psalmist's way when his spirit is faint.

The psalm ends with the righteous gathering around the rescued man. God's deliverance is meant to be celebrated in community, and the lonely man's restoration includes being restored to the company of God's people.

words.note: Siach, complaint or musing. The word can describe a meditation, a lament, or an anxious complaint poured out. Verse 2 uses it for the psalmist's troubled speech before God. It shows that the Psalms welcome not only calm reflection but also distressed, even repetitive, outpouring.

Cheleq, portion or share. The word describes an allotted share, especially of land or inheritance. The Levites had no land portion because the LORD was their portion. When the psalmist calls God his portion in the land of the living, he says that God himself is his inheritance and security in this life, not only after it.

Manos, refuge or place of escape. The word describes a place to flee to. In verse 4 the psalmist says there is none for him. In verse 5 he uses a related word, calling the LORD his refuge. The turn from one to the other is the heart of the psalm.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 142, but its picture of a man abandoned by all, with no one at his right hand, finds a deep echo in the story of Jesus. At his arrest all the disciples deserted him and fled (Mark 14:50), and he faced his trial alone. Like David in the cave, Jesus was hunted by the powerful, yet he did not seize power to save himself. The psalm's confession that the LORD is my portion in the land of the living expresses the trust Jesus lived out, and its hope that the righteous will gather around the one who is set free finds its fulfillment in the church gathered around the risen Christ. The link is thematic rather than predictive, but it shows the rejected king of the psalm and the rejected Son of David walking the same road.
questions: The psalmist says no one cares for his soul. Have you ever felt that alone, and what did you do with that feeling?
What would it mean for God to be your portion, your share and inheritance, when other securities are gone?
The psalm ends with the righteous gathering around the rescued man. Who in your life needs you to gather around them right now?
